66186276B48953429733047.name: Idaho
66186276B48953429733047.summary: The strictest criminal facility ban in the country: HB 752 (effective 1 July 2026) makes it a crime — misdemeanour up to 1 year, felony up to 5 years on a second offence within five years — for a trans person to use a restroom or changing room matching their gender identity in government buildings and all private businesses open to the public (gas stations, restaurants, hospitals). A federal court partially blocked it, but it remains in effect wherever no gender-neutral option exists. Four successive legislative rounds (2023–2026) plus a pride-flag ban; rated “Do Not Travel” in the July 2026 legal-risk assessment. Well below the national score 0.36.

66186276B41335105066757.name: Louisiana
66186276B41335105066757.summary: The highest measured killing rate in the country (24.7 per 100k trans women/yr) and a damning institutional response: after a mob of ~10 beat a trans couple outside a women's restroom in Benton (May 2026), no alleged attacker was arrested and both victims were criminally charged, one booked into a men's facility. The same parish municipality moved to criminalise trans restroom use by local ordinance — the sharpest instrument in a state with no statewide adult ban. A trans inmate was killed at Angola state prison (2024); killings continue into 2026. Well below the national score 0.36.

66186276B29106115751815.name: Texas
66186276B29106115751815.summary: The facility ban (SB 8, effective Dec 2025) is actually enforced: within 48 hours, state troopers checked IDs at women's restrooms in the Capitol and issued criminal-trespass warnings to four trans women with one-year Capitol bans; the AG has since opened enforcement inquiries against a school district (escalated April 2026) and a university student was formally investigated. Highest absolute toll of killings of trans women in the country (44 recorded 2008–2025; 7.6 per 100k/yr); 66 anti-LGBTQ incidents in 2025 (3rd-highest). Rated “Do Not Travel.” Well below the national score 0.36.

66186276B52324970173776.name: Tennessee
66186276B52324970173776.summary: The only state with a standing criminal ban on gender-expressive performance: the Adult Entertainment Act (2023) criminalises “male or female impersonation” in public or where a child might be present — settled law after the 6th Circuit reversed the invalidating ruling (July 2024) and SCOTUS denied review (Feb 2025), so it is enforceable against a visitor presenting in drag. A 2019 amendment widened the indecent-exposure statute; 7.8 killings per 100k trans women/yr, above the general US homicide rate. Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B64014601259366.name: Kansas
66186276B64014601259366.summary: SB 244 (enacted Feb 2026 over the governor's veto) confines trans people to birth-sex facilities in government buildings and creates a private right of action letting anyone sue a person they suspect of violating it for ~$1,000 — a bounty-hunter mechanism that exposes visitors directly. It also invalidates Kansas-issued IDs with corrected markers. First state designated “Do Not Travel” in the current assessment cycle; two trans men sued within days citing fear of violence. Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B69138566591314.name: Mississippi
66186276B69138566591314.summary: Facility bans enacted 2024 and 2025 and a statutory birth-sex definition place it in the worst-law group. One important counterweight: the justice system does prosecute — the killer of a trans woman in Lucedale received 49 years in federal prison for a bias-motivated murder, positive evidence about institutional response rather than about risk level. Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B83300161667341.name: Oklahoma
66186276B83300161667341.summary: Facility bans 2022 and 2025 plus a statutory birth-sex definition of “sex.” Large parts of the state are Public Law 280 tribal jurisdiction, where gender-recognition law varies by nation and cannot be scored at this level. Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B98021244841737.name: Alabama
66186276B98021244841737.summary: Facility bans 2022 and 2024, with the “Don't Say Gay” law extending bathroom restrictions to college campuses; 3.8 killings per 100k trans women/yr. Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B82803899326534.name: Indiana
66186276B82803899326534.summary: 2026 criminal-penalty and ID laws placed it “among the harshest anti-trans states” in the February 2026 assessment; criminal-charge exposure for bathroom use has been flagged since 2023, and it appears on the 2026 enacted-lists (flagged: that tracker renders client-side and could not be re-verified at the URL). Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B31593004124297.name: Utah
66186276B31593004124297.summary: First state to criminalise adult restroom use (HB 257, 2024) — not just school facilities — and first to explicitly prohibit LGBTQ flags at government buildings and schools (May 2025, fines up to $500/day). Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B22881275445497.name: North Dakota
66186276B22881275445497.summary: HB 1259 (2025) facility ban; birth-sex definition in statute. In the worst-law group per the July 2026 legal-risk assessment. Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B38006515706420.name: South Dakota
66186276B38006515706420.summary: 2025 facility ban; birth-sex definition in statute. In the worst-law group per the July 2026 legal-risk assessment. Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B10933057601622.name: Wyoming
66186276B10933057601622.summary: Two facility bills signed March 2025; birth-sex definition in statute. In the worst-law group per the July 2026 legal-risk assessment. Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B64762166704956.name: West Virginia
66186276B64762166704956.summary: March 2025 facility ban with unusually wide reach: K-12, higher education, corrections and domestic-violence shelters. In the worst-law group per the July 2026 legal-risk assessment. Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B86295910312663.name: Arkansas
66186276B86295910312663.summary: HB 1156 (2023, K-12 facilities) extended 2025. School-focused, so traveler exposure is narrower than in adult-reaching bans. In the worst-law group per the July 2026 legal-risk assessment. Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B76680759932915.name: Ohio
66186276B76680759932915.summary: 2024 facility ban. In the worst-law group per the July 2026 legal-risk assessment. Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B63937528568220.name: Iowa
66186276B63937528568220.summary: Facility ban enacted; appears on 2026 enacted-lists (flagged: client-side tracker, not re-verifiable at URL). In the worst-law group per the July 2026 legal-risk assessment. Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B79689460185872.name: South Carolina
66186276B79689460185872.summary: 2024 facility ban expanded in 2026 to colleges and universities, raising its tier to “Worst Laws Passed” in the July 2026 assessment; part of the 18-state birth-sex-definition group. Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B65591139260314.name: Florida
66186276B65591139260314.summary: § 553.865 (2023) makes refusing to leave a facility not matching sex assigned at birth — after being told by a government employee — criminal trespass in state-owned buildings. Produced what is believed to be the first arrest under a state trans bathroom law (March 2025, Capitol, held ~24h; charges later dismissed on a technicality — a mixed-leaning-positive institutional response). The state stopped issuing corrected-marker licences and treats “misrepresentation” as potential fraud; Equality Florida and HRC issued named travel advisories. Physical safety is comparatively better than the law suggests: 3.7 killings per 100k trans women/yr, below the worst-law average. Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B73402293045483.name: Nebraska
66186276B73402293045483.summary: Gubernatorial executive order narrowing “male”/“female” and ending state recognition of trans people — mostly resident-facing, but it signals an administration willing to use state machinery against gender identity. Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B22971435435932.name: Kentucky
66186276B22971435435932.summary: 2023 K-12 facility ban; school-focused, so direct traveler exposure is limited, but it places the state in the banning group. Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B6801956407400.name: North Carolina
66186276B6801956407400.summary: The archetype of this tier's instability: HB 2 (2016) restricted bathrooms to birth-certificate sex and was repealed in 2017 after mass backlash, but a binary-“sex” statute remains and 12 killings are recorded (6.4 per 100k trans women/yr, above the general homicide rate). Below the national score 0.36.

66186276B80192890672447.name: Montana
66186276B80192890672447.summary: HB 121 (2025) facility ban plus a pride-flag ban — but laws that would normally place it among the worst states have repeatedly been blocked in court, and it was the one state improving in the February 2026 assessment. Statutory risk is high; enforcement risk is genuinely mixed. Slightly below the national score 0.36.

66186276B13694661525286.name: Missouri
66186276B13694661525286.summary: Bans gender-affirming care for incarcerated adults as well as minors (resident-facing, but signals institutional posture); no adult facility ban recorded. Slightly below the national score 0.36.

66186276B62688952876525.name: Alaska
66186276B62688952876525.summary: Moderate tier in the July 2026 assessment: no adult facility ban recorded, no protective statute. Slightly below the national score 0.36.

66186276B75419826371250.name: Georgia
66186276B75419826371250.summary: No state facility ban, but Atlanta is a long-run concentration point for killings of trans people (≥15 fatal cases 1990–2014, 16 more 2015–2023; 4.8 per 100k trans women/yr), and Columbus Pride cancelled its 2026 Diversity Saturday because it could not secure off-duty officers — security forces unwilling to be visibly associated. Slightly below the national score 0.36.

66186276B86627915353587.name: New Hampshire
66186276B86627915353587.summary: Highest per-capita incident load in the country: 72 recorded anti-LGBTQ incidents in 2025 in a state of ~1.4m. Counterweight: in July 2026 a county court found an attacker violated the NH Civil Rights Act after striking a trans gas-station employee, using his pronoun refusal as bias evidence, with bodycam showing officers correcting his pronoun use — institutions working. Slightly below the national score 0.36.

66186276B89395128410123.name: Arizona
66186276B89395128410123.summary: “Low Risk” tier in the July 2026 assessment — largely refrains from targeting trans adults without specialising in protection; Tucson cancelled its 2026 Pride citing the political and financial climate. Appears on 2026 enacted-lists (flagged: client-side tracker). Around the national score 0.36.

66186276B53580985925186.name: Virginia
66186276B53580985925186.summary: “Low Risk” tier, but enacted a K-12 facility ban in 2023 (school-focused; limited traveler exposure). Around the national score 0.36.

66186276B94082813086253.name: District of Columbia
66186276B94082813086253.summary: Downgraded from “most protective”: as a federal district, Congress and the executive reach it directly — Congress attached a bathroom ban for DC, and activists protesting it at the Capitol were arrested (Dec 2024). Its protective local law layer persists but is overridable. Around the national score 0.36.

66186276B78821008370123.name: Maine
66186276B78821008370123.summary: “Low Risk” tier, but rose in risk after the University of Maine system capitulated to federal pressure on trans sports participation — an institution folding rather than defending. Around the national score 0.36.

66186276B31549545599635.name: Delaware
66186276B31549545599635.summary: “Low Risk” tier in the July 2026 assessment: largely refrains from targeting trans adults but does not specialise in protection; no state-specific finding beyond the shared tier evidence. Marginally above the national score 0.36.

66186276B6628180846672.name: Pennsylvania
66186276B6628180846672.summary: “Low Risk” tier in the July 2026 assessment: largely refrains from targeting trans adults but does not specialise in protection; no state-specific finding beyond the shared tier evidence. Marginally above the national score 0.36.

66186276B91272823970344.name: Wisconsin
66186276B91272823970344.summary: “Low Risk” tier in the July 2026 assessment: largely refrains from targeting trans adults but does not specialise in protection; no state-specific finding beyond the shared tier evidence. Marginally above the national score 0.36.

66186276B37442548568489.name: Michigan
66186276B37442548568489.summary: Mixed: robust anti-discrimination protections codified (2023 bipartisan expansion), but the state is not protecting incarcerated trans people. Direction genuinely two-sided. Above the national score 0.36.

66186276B98615608994420.name: Nevada
66186276B98615608994420.summary: Mixed-leaning-protective: gender identity added to the state constitution by 2022 ballot; “Most Protective”-adjacent tier. Above the national score 0.36.

66186276B21291522594454.name: Maryland
66186276B21291522594454.summary: The clearest law-violence divergence in the country: Trans Health Equity Act and refuge/shield protections (Most Protective tier), and the second-highest killing rate (11.1 per 100k trans women/yr), including two Black trans women shot dead in Baltimore ten weeks apart in 2026. Protective law does not by itself make people safer. Above the national score 0.36, capped by the violence data.

66186276B43071933723331.name: California
66186276B43071933723331.summary: Highest legal floor in the country: first sanctuary-state law (SB 107, 2023) and shield protections against out-of-state enforcement. But also the most incidents of any state in 2025 (198, GLAAD ALERT) with a “dramatic increase” in LA hate crime, and 34 recorded killings 2008–2025 (4.1 per 100k). Above the national score 0.36; law and street volume pull opposite ways.

66186276B35012827062242.name: Colorado
66186276B35012827062242.summary: CADA expressly covers gender identity and expression in employment, housing and public accommodation — the last is directly traveler-relevant (hotels, restaurants, venues) — expanded again in 2025. Most Protective tier. Clearly above the national score 0.36.

66186276B10610315112087.name: Minnesota
66186276B10610315112087.summary: Went furthest on non-cooperation: HF 146 (2023) declares out-of-state anti-trans law “against the public policy of this state” and blocks out-of-state warrants, arrests and extradition related to gender-affirming care — a state refusing to enforce other states' hostility. Most Protective tier; among the safest legal environments for a trans visitor in the US. Clearly above the national score 0.36.

66186276B73434888205604.name: New Jersey
66186276B73434888205604.summary: The safest measured jurisdiction in the country: lowest per-capita killing rate in the state-by-state dataset (3.4 per 100k trans women/yr; 4 recorded deaths 2008–2025) — half the general US homicide rate — inside the Most Protective legal tier. Clearly above the national score 0.36.

66186276B83663796884405.summary: “Most Protective” tier in the July 2026 assessment: regional non-discrimination covering gender identity and shield/refuge protections enforceable against out-of-state actions; no state-specific negative finding beyond the shared federal layer (passport/API policy, priced into the national score). Clearly above the national score 0.36.
